newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Mercedes chief says trucks to boost sales.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mercedes chief says trucks to boost sales.

text.p: Mercedes-Benz chairman Helmut Werner said on Thursday he expected the German truck and carmaker to report 1996 sales of about 75 billion marks ($49.66 billion), boosted by its commercial vehicle unit.
Werner told a news conference at the IAA truck exhibition that Mercedes, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, saw total sales rise nine percent in the first eight months of the year to 50.9 billion marks.
He forecast "record sales" at the company's commercial vehicle unit, topping the 320,000 vehicles sold in 1995 despite Germany's economic woes.
"Expanding our commercial vehicle business unit will be one of the main focal points for the further development of our company."
Mercedes is earning a profit from sales of transporters and buses, but Werner said the company "has a fight on our hands" in the market for trucks over six tonnes.
Werner said commercial vehicle sales during the first eight months of 1996 were up six percent over year-ago levels, reaching 221,000 vehicles worldwide.
"In view of our success on the passenger car side, some people may overlook the fact that we have sold more commercial vehicles this year than ever before in our history," he said.

Athough Werner said Mercedes "has developed according to plan in every respect" so far during 1996, Europe's truck market has been brutal and many makers have had to offer generous deals to maintain market share.

The strain on Mercedes, Europe's truck market leader, showed in August when Bernd Gottschalk resigned as head of the commercial division. Company officials said he had disagreed with other executives over the unit's strategy.
Werner also described the business trend in the bus, coach and van sectors as "exceptionally positive".
Mercedes was enjoying varied success in Europe, he said. While orders in the German commercial vehicle market were beginning to pick up again, business in the rest of Europe was starting to flag.
Werner also said the reorganisation of Mercedes' European bus units under Setra and Mercedes-Benz was showing benefits.
Sales of more than 3,500 buses weighing more than eight tonnes during the first eight months of 1996 exceeded year-ago sales by about 28 percent.
"Having made losses in the European bus market for many years, our Evobus operations are now showing results," he said.

In the van sector, Werner said Mercedes was "enjoying particular success" both in terms of sales figures and incoming orders. Mercedes sold 76,500 units, increasing its van sales in the west European market by 26 percent.
Mercedes, set to unveil its Vito and Sprinter vans, said it now has a European market share in the van class of 14 percent, about 2.2 percentage points higher than year-ago levels.
At its U.S. subsidiary Freightliner, Werner said sales were up 10 percent despite what he called a crumbling U.S. market.
In Latin America, Werner said Mercedes truck units in Argentina and Brazil have made a comeback against the backdrop of what he believed was sustained economic development.
But he warned the worst is yet to come in Brazil. The market was in "exceptionally poor state of health" and sales at Mercedes-Benz do Brazil were down one-third from 1995 levels.
Werner said Mercedes was interested in the Chinese market, noting the recent announcement of a coach-building joint venture in the Chinese province of Yangzhou. ($1=1.5103 Mark)
